Nosferatu. An unauthorized 1922 adaptation of Bram Stoker's Dracula, this is F.W. Murnau's masterwork of atmospheric horror. Using German Expressionist shadows and grotesque design, it follows the parasitic Count Orlok's curse spreading from Transylvania to a Baltic port town, establishing the visual language and psychological terror of vampire cinema.

Count Orlok is cinema's first iconic vampire: skeletal, rat-like, moving with unnatural jerks. Actor Max Schreck's performance remains unsettling. The film uses extreme chiaroscuro—sharp contrasts between light and shadow—and distorted set design to create psychological dread without gore. Shadows of Orlok climbing stairs terrify more than explicit violence ever could.

Murnau employed innovative techniques throughout. Negative film creates supernatural effects. Iris shots isolate dread. A slow, deliberate pacing builds mounting inevitability. The film's plot follows Hutter, a real-estate agent who travels to Transylvania, unknowingly facilitates Orlok's journey to the West, and watches the vampire consume his town and his wife.

Nosferatu influenced virtually every vampire film after it. Orlok's visual design remains the template for horror iconography. The film was nearly erased entirely—Stoker's widow sued and won the right to destroy copies—but restoration in the nineteen sixties preserved it. The production history itself became legend. Nosferatu has become a cornerstone of cinema history and horror canon, and fellow Expressionist masterpieces like The Cabinet of Dr. Caligari, released four years earlier, share its use of shadow and distortion as the visual grammar of the unconscious mind.
